title: Was I Addicted to the Struggle
author: Summer Mulder
summary: The follow-up to Mulder's first Substack post examines why she spent years unable to hear advice she did not dispute. Her husband had gently pointed to a bigger opportunity, one they already shared and which was compounding at twenty times the rate of the business that was hers alone, but taking it would have meant conceding she had been wrong. The essay's diagnosis is that the business had become an identity rather than an asset, the repository of her belief that she was smart, strong and worthy enough to build something alone. She distinguishes the erosion that comes when your heart leaves the work from burnout caused by overwork, and makes the case that quitting the right thing is sometimes what allows you to avoid quitting everything. A useful contrast runs through the piece between building to align and building to prove, with resistance described as fighting against something rather than for it and showing up as irritability, defensiveness and exhaustion. Mulder is honest that most of her lessons have been slow burns rather than lightning bolts, and that no one can be rushed through them. She ends on a reframe rather than advice: what if the opportunity lies in what you are avoiding rather than what you are forcing.
points: Mulder's key mechanism is that doubling down was never about the numbers, since letting go would have meant admitting she had been wrong, which made persistence a face-saving strategy.
The distinction she draws between burnout from overwork and erosion from a departed heart matters practically, because the two conditions call for opposite responses.
Her rule that quitting the right thing prevents quitting everything is an unusually clean formulation from someone who explicitly does not believe in quitting easily.
Resistance is given observable symptoms, irritability, defensiveness and exhaustion, so it can be detected rather than merely felt.
She notes the release that follows a decision arrives before any external circumstances change, with clarity about how problems will be solved rather than solutions themselves.
quotes: And whenever something stopped working, or the numbers started slipping, I didn’t let go.
And it was happening at a 20x rate compared to the one that was just mine.
There came a point when I stopped waking up with excitement and started waking up with anxiety.
Building to align vs. building to prove holds a completely different energy.
What if the opportunity isn’t in what you’re forcing, but in what you’re avoiding?
And it takes a hell of a lot of grace to admit you were wrong… and start again, wiser.
